Exeter.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Exeter and East Devon
s1loc: Exeter anchors a busy Devon visitor economy around Exeter Cathedral, one of the great Gothic churches of England with its roof and tower tours, and the free Royal Albert Memorial Museum (RAMM) on Queen Street. The Underground Passages, the Roman city wall and the historic Exeter Quayside on the River Exe draw steady year-round footfall, with Powderham Castle and its deer park just beyond the city.

The leisure and activity layer runs from the Quay, where kayak, paddleboard and cycle hire work the Exe estuary and the canal towpath, out to the wider Exe Valley. Family draws include Crealy Theme Park and Resort at Clyst St Mary, the RHS Garden Rosemoor trade and Haldon Forest Park, while the Riverside Leisure Centre and waterside operators stay busy through the warmer season.

Heritage and culture centre on the Cathedral Green and the medieval Guildhall, with Northernhay and Rougemont Gardens, the Royal Clarence and the Custom House quarter. The Northcott Theatre, the Phoenix arts centre and Exeter Corn Exchange carry the events calendar, alongside Gandy Street, the Princesshay quarter and a programme of festivals that fill the city through spring and summer.

Underpinning it all is a deep hotel and guesthouse base across the city centre and the Exe estuary villages, plus a tour-operator and guiding scene working the Cathedral, Quayside and Dartmoor day trips. Exeter St Davids and Exeter Central stations and Exeter Airport bring visitors in, with Exmouth, Topsham and the Jurassic Coast a short hop for the seasonal draw.

Solihull.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Solihull
s1loc: Solihull sits at the heart of the West Midlands visitor economy, home to the National Exhibition Centre (NEC), Resorts World Birmingham and the arena cluster that pulls millions of event visitors a year. The historic High Street, St Alphege Church and the Touchwood centre give the town a strong core, while the village of Knowle and its Grand Union Canal locks add timber-framed charm just outside the centre.

The leisure and activity layer runs from Malvern and Brueton Park, with its nature centre and lake, out to Elmdon Park and Tudor Grange Park. Tudor Grange Leisure Centre, the Hatchford Brook and Olton Mere green spaces and the canal walks around Catherine-de-Barnes keep families and activity operators working, alongside the indoor venues clustered around Resorts World and the NEC throughout the season.

Heritage and culture take in the medieval St Alphege Church, Berry Hall and the conservation streets of Knowle and Dorridge, with the Core Theatre at the heart of the town's events calendar. Packwood House and Baddesley Clinton, two well-known National Trust houses, sit close by, and the arena programme at Resorts World and the NEC complex keep the cultural draw strong.

Underpinning it all is one of the region's deepest hotel bases, with the Hilton, Crowne Plaza, Holiday Inn and Genting hotels serving the NEC and the airport. Birmingham Airport, Birmingham International station and the M42 corridor bring conference, concert and exhibition visitors in, with Stratford-upon-Avon, the Warwickshire countryside and the city centre all an easy day trip away.

Colchester.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Colchester
s1loc: Colchester, Britain's oldest recorded town and Roman capital, builds its visitor economy around Colchester Castle, Europe's largest Norman keep, set in Castle Park with its Roman vaults and rooftop tours. Firstsite, the striking golden gallery, the Roman wall and Balkerne Gate, and the Dutch Quarter give the city a deep historic core that draws visitors across the year to the heart of north Essex.

The leisure and activity layer is led by Colchester Zoo, one of the region's biggest family draws with its lions, elephants and big cats, alongside Castle Park, Highwoods Country Park and Cudmore Grove on the nearby Mersea coast. Leisure World Colchester, the boating lake and the watersports and sailing scene around the Colne estuary keep operators busy through the warmer months.

Heritage and culture run from the Hollytrees Museum, a Georgian house in Castle Park, to the Roman Circus, the Minories and the historic High Street. The Mercury Theatre and the Charter Hall at Colchester Arts Centre carry a packed events calendar, with the Colchester Free Festival, the food and military tattoo events and the garrison heritage adding to the seasonal programme.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and guesthouse base across the town centre and the garrison, plus a guiding and tour scene built on the Roman and military story. Colchester and Colchester Town stations on the main line to London Liverpool Street bring day-trippers in fast, with Mersea Island, Dedham Vale and Constable Country a short drive for the seasonal draw.

Cheltenham.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Cheltenham and the Cotswolds
s1loc: Cheltenham, the most complete Regency town in the country, builds its visitor economy around the Promenade and Montpellier, the Pittville Pump Room and the grand spa-town architecture that draws visitors all year. The Wilson Art Gallery and Museum, the Imperial Gardens and the elegant terraces give the town a cultural core, with the wider Cotswolds making it a major gateway for day visitors and holidaymakers.

The leisure and activity layer centres on Pittville Park, with its boating lake, aviaries and skate park, and Sandford Park with its open-air lido. Montpellier Gardens, the Honeybourne cycle line and the Leisure at Cheltenham centre keep families and activity operators working, while Cleeve Hill and the Cotswold Way on the doorstep draw walkers and riders through the season.

Heritage and culture make Cheltenham a festival town, home to the Cheltenham Literature, Jazz, Science and Music Festivals that fill the Town Hall and the Everyman Theatre with international names. The Wilson, the Holst Victorian House and the Regency squares anchor the heritage offer, with a packed events calendar spanning the Promenade, Imperial Gardens and Montpellier across spring and summer.

Underpinning it all is Cheltenham Racecourse, host of the world-famous Cheltenham Festival each March, plus a deep hotel and guesthouse base across Montpellier and the Promenade. A strong tour-operator and guiding scene works the Cotswolds, with Cheltenham Spa station and the M5 bringing visitors in and Gloucester, the Forest of Dean and the Cotswold villages all an easy day trip.

Gateshead.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Gateshead and Tyneside
s1loc: Gateshead anchors a major Tyneside visitor economy around the Angel of the North, Antony Gormley's twenty-metre landmark, and the regenerated Gateshead Quays on the River Tyne. The Gateshead Millennium Bridge, the Baltic Centre for Contemporary Art in its converted flour mill and the curving Glasshouse International Centre for Music form a cultural waterfront that draws visitors across the year.

The leisure and activity layer runs from the MetroCentre, one of Europe's largest covered shopping and leisure centres with its climbing and mini-golf, to Saltwell Park, the town's grand Victorian green space. Watersports and rowing on the Tyne, the Gateshead International Stadium and the trails of the Derwent Walk Country Park keep families and activity operators working through the warmer season.

Heritage and culture take in St Mary's Heritage Centre by the river, the Shipley Art Gallery and the historic Saltwell Towers, alongside the Sage-era music programme now at the Glasshouse. The Baltic's rotating exhibitions, the Quays festival calendar and the major events at Gateshead International Stadium carry a strong cultural draw across the spring and summer events season.

Underpinning it all is a hotel base across the Quays and the MetroCentre, plus a guiding and tour scene built on the NewcastleGateshead waterfront. The Tyne and Wear Metro, Newcastle Central station and Newcastle International Airport bring visitors in fast, with the Northumberland coast, Beamish and the Durham countryside all within easy reach for the seasonal day-trip draw.

High Wycombe.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of High Wycombe and the Chilterns
s1loc: High Wycombe anchors a Chilterns visitor economy around Hughenden Manor, Benjamin Disraeli's National Trust country house, and the dramatic Hellfire Caves at West Wycombe, a chalk-and-flint network running 260 metres underground. West Wycombe Park, the Dashwood mausoleum and St Lawrence's golden-ball church on the hill above give the town a strong historic draw across the wooded southern Chilterns.

The leisure and activity layer runs from The Rye, the town's riverside park with its lido and boating, out to Hughenden Valley and the Chiltern beech woods. Wycombe Rye Lido, the Wycombe Heights and the activity centres along the Chilterns Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty keep walkers, cyclists and family operators busy, with Bekonscot and the wider valley trails busy through the warmer season.

Heritage and culture take in the historic Guildhall and the Little Market House, the Wycombe Museum and the town's chair-making heritage in the High Street. The Wycombe Swan Theatre carries the events calendar with touring shows and pantomime, alongside the National Trust programme at Hughenden and West Wycombe and a calendar of village fetes and festivals across the Chilterns.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and inn base across the town and the surrounding villages, plus a guiding scene built on the Chiltern hills and the National Trust houses. High Wycombe station, twenty minutes from London Marylebone, and the M40 make it a strong day-trip hub, with the Chilterns, Marlow and the Thames Valley all close for the seasonal draw.

Blackburn.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Blackburn and East Lancashire
s1loc: Blackburn anchors an East Lancashire visitor economy around Blackburn Cathedral, one of England's newest cathedrals and home to the largest collection of modern religious art in the country, set in the heart of the town. The Blackburn Museum and Art Gallery, with its textiles, looms and rare books, and the landmark Darwen Tower on the moors above add a strong heritage draw across the season.

The leisure and activity layer is led by Witton Country Park, 480 acres of trails, nature walks and play areas with a visitor centre, alongside Corporation Park and the moors above Darwen. Blackburn Ice Arena, the Witton athletics and leisure facilities and the walking and cycling routes onto Darwen Moor and the West Pennine Moors keep families and activity operators working through the warmer months.

Heritage and culture take in the cotton-town story told at the museum, the Cotton Exchange and the historic market, alongside the conservation streets around the Cathedral quarter. King George's Hall, the town's Grade II listed concert venue, carries the events calendar with concerts, pantomime and live shows, with festivals and markets filling the town centre across the spring and summer events season.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and guesthouse base across the town and the surrounding hills, plus a guiding scene built on the Pennine moors and the cotton heritage. Blackburn station, the M65 and the Ribble Valley make it a base for visitors, with Darwen, Accrington and the Forest of Bowland and Ribble Valley all close for the seasonal day-trip draw.
